```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4
)
set.seed(20260529)
source(system.file("knitr/fit-cache.R", package = "tulpa"))
```

`mode = "smc"` fits a model with a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler: a
population of particles is moved step by step from a reference distribution
to the posterior. The weights collected along the way estimate the log
evidence $\log p(y)$. The path can also stop at the posterior tempered at
inverse temperature `1 / log(n)`, and the draws recorded there give the widely
applicable Bayesian information criterion (WBIC) of Watanabe (2013), a second
estimate of the negative log evidence. This article fits a Gaussian linear
model whose posterior, evidence and WBIC have closed forms, checks the SMC fit
against all three, compares SMC with NUTS on a Poisson model, and ends with
nested models ranked by both estimates. Installation is covered in
[Get started](tulpa.html); the inference tiers are described in
[Inference modes](inference-modes.html), and the evidence of a Laplace fit,
WAIC and LOO in [Model comparison](model-comparison.html).

1. **Fit** with `tulpa(..., mode = "smc", control = list(wbic = TRUE))`.
2. **Check** the draws with `coef()`, `summary()` and `confint()`.
3. **Read** the log evidence with `logLik()` and the criterion with `wbic()`.
4. **Rank** candidate models with `compare_models()`.

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)
```

## How the sampler moves its particles

The sampler carries 1,000 particles along a path of distributions from a
reference to the posterior. The reference is fitted to the posterior in two
steps. A Pathfinder normal approximation starts a first pass on a quarter of
the particles, and a multivariate t distribution with 3 degrees of freedom,
located and scaled by the mean and covariance of the population that pass ends
with, is the reference of the run that reports. At each step of that run the
sampler picks the next point on the path so that the effective sample size of
the reweighted population stays at half the particle count, resamples the
particles to equal weights, and moves them until they have decorrelated from
the resampled start. The draws a fit returns are the final population, equally
weighted, so the fit carries no chains and `summary()` reports no Rhat.

With `control = list(wbic = TRUE)` the path has two legs. The first ends at
the tempered posterior
$p_\beta(\theta) \propto p(\theta) \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i \mid \theta)^\beta$
with $\beta = 1 / \log n$, where the population is stored. The second leg
raises the likelihood power from $\beta$ to 1, so the fit's posterior draws are
the same kind of draws as without the option.

## A model with a known posterior

The data are 200 observations of a response `y` with three covariates: `x`
(true slope 1.0), `z` (true slope 0.3) and `w`, which has no effect. The
intercept is 0.5 and the residual standard deviation is 0.8.

```{r sim}
set.seed(3)
n <- 200
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n), z = rnorm(n), w = rnorm(n))
d$y <- 0.5 + 1.0 * d$x + 0.3 * d$z + rnorm(n, sd = 0.8)
```

With the residual variance held at its true value, `phi = 0.64`, and a normal
prior with mean 0 and SD 2 on every coefficient, the posterior of the
coefficients is Gaussian and its mean and covariance have a closed form.
`exact_posterior()` returns both.

```{r exact-post}
phi <- 0.64
s   <- 2
exact_posterior <- function(X, y, beta = 1) {
  P <- beta * crossprod(X) / phi + diag(ncol(X)) / s^2
  V <- chol2inv(chol(P))
  m <- V %*% (beta * crossprod(X, y) / phi)
  list(mean = drop(m), V = V)
}
X_xz <- model.matrix(~ x + z, d)
ep <- exact_posterior(X_xz, d$y)
```

The SMC fit uses the same residual variance and prior. `seed` fixes the
sampler's random stream; `n_particles` is set to its default to make it
visible.

```{r fit-smc, fit = c("fit_xz")}
fit_xz <- tulpa(y ~ x + z, data = d, family = "gaussian", mode = "smc",
                phi = phi, beta_prior = list(mean = 0, sd = s),
                control = list(wbic = TRUE, n_particles = 1000L,
                               seed = 1L))
```

`coef(summary())` gives the posterior mean and SD of each coefficient from the
draws. Next to the closed form:

```{r post-table}
sm <- coef(summary(fit_xz))
data.frame(row.names  = rownames(sm),
           smc_mean   = round(sm[, "estimate"], 4),
           exact_mean = round(ep$mean, 4),
           smc_sd     = round(sm[, "std.error"], 4),
           exact_sd   = round(sqrt(diag(ep$V)), 4))
```

The SMC means differ from the exact ones by at most
`r signif(max(abs(sm[, "estimate"] - ep$mean)), 2)` and the SDs by at most
`r signif(max(abs(sm[, "std.error"] - sqrt(diag(ep$V)))), 2)`. The Monte Carlo
standard error of a mean from 1,000 independent draws is about 0.002 here (an
SD of 0.056 over the square root of 1,000). The path of this fit had
`r length(fit_xz$n_moves)` steps, and `fit_xz$n_moves` holds the number of
moves made at each: `r paste(fit_xz$n_moves, collapse = ", ")`.

## SMC against NUTS

On a non-Gaussian model there is no closed form to check against, so the
reference is a NUTS fit (`mode = "hmc"`) of the same model. The data are 150
Poisson counts with intercept 0.3 and slope 0.6 on the log scale; both fits use
the default prior.

```{r sim-pois, fit = c("dp", "fit_smc", "fit_nuts")}
set.seed(4)
dp <- data.frame(x = rnorm(150))
dp$y <- rpois(150, exp(0.3 + 0.6 * dp$x))
fit_smc <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = dp, family = "poisson", mode = "smc",
                 control = list(seed = 1L))
fit_nuts <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = dp, family = "poisson", mode = "hmc",
                  control = list(seed = 1L))
```

```{r pois-ci}
ci <- rbind(smc = confint(fit_smc)["x", ], nuts = confint(fit_nuts)["x", ])
ci
```

Both 95% intervals for the slope cover 0.6. Their ends differ by
`r round(abs(diff(ci[, 1])), 3)` and `r round(abs(diff(ci[, 2])), 3)`, against
a posterior SD of the slope of
`r round(sd(as_draws_matrix(fit_nuts)[, "x"]), 2)`. The figure sets the slope
draws of the two samplers against each other: SMC's 1,000 particles and the
`r format(nrow(as_draws_matrix(fit_nuts)), big.mark = ",")` NUTS draws.

```{r pois-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Left: overlaid density curves of the slope draws from SMC and NUTS, nearly identical, with a vertical line at the simulated slope of 0.6. Right: quantile-quantile plot of SMC against NUTS slope draws lying on the identity line."}
b_smc  <- as_draws_matrix(fit_smc)[, "x"]
b_nuts <- as_draws_matrix(fit_nuts)[, "x"]
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(density(b_nuts), main = "", xlab = "slope", lwd = 2)
lines(density(b_smc), lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "darkorange")
abline(v = 0.6, col = "grey50")
legend("topright", c("NUTS", "SMC"), lty = 1:2, lwd = 2,
       col = c("black", "darkorange"), bty = "n")
qq <- qqplot(b_nuts, b_smc, plot.it = FALSE)
plot(qq, pch = 20, xlab = "NUTS quantiles", ylab = "SMC quantiles")
abline(0, 1, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
par(op)
```

The densities overlap and the quantiles lie on the identity line out to the
tails, so the SMC population and the NUTS chains describe the same posterior.

## The evidence

`logLik()` on an SMC fit is the log evidence, and says so in its `quantity`
attribute. It is the sum over the steps of the path of the log mean
incremental weight, plus the normalizing constants of the prior and the
likelihood. The `mc_se` attribute is its Monte Carlo standard error.

```{r loglik}
ll <- logLik(fit_xz)
ll
attr(ll, "quantity")
attr(ll, "mc_se")
```

For this model the evidence has a closed form: with the coefficients
integrated out, `y` is distributed as $N(0, \phi I + s^2 X X^\top)$.

```{r exact-evidence}
neg_log_evidence <- function(X, y) {
  L <- chol(phi * diag(length(y)) + s^2 * tcrossprod(X))
  length(y) / 2 * log(2 * pi) + sum(log(diag(L))) +
    sum(backsolve(L, y, transpose = TRUE)^2) / 2
}
c(smc = as.numeric(ll), exact = -neg_log_evidence(X_xz, d$y))
```

```{r evidence-numbers, include = FALSE}
ev_gap <- as.numeric(ll) + neg_log_evidence(X_xz, d$y)
```

The SMC estimate is `r round(abs(ev_gap), 2)`
`r if (ev_gap > 0) "above" else "below"` the exact log evidence,
`r round(abs(ev_gap) / attr(ll, "mc_se"), 1)` of its standard errors. The
standard error counts the variance of the weights over independent particles
and leaves out the correlation the moves leave between particles
(`?logLik.tulpa_fit`).

## WBIC against the exact evidence

`wbic()` reads the population stored at $\beta = 1 / \log n$ and averages the
negative log-likelihood over it:

$$
\mathrm{WBIC} = -E_\beta\Big[\sum_{i=1}^n \log p(y_i \mid \theta)\Big].
$$

It estimates the negative log evidence $-\log p(y)$, and lower is better.

```{r wbic}
wbic(fit_xz)
```

For the Gaussian model the WBIC has a closed form as well. The tempered
posterior is Gaussian too (`exact_posterior()` with `beta`), so the expectation
above can be written out.

```{r exact-wbic}
exact_wbic <- function(X, y) {
  tp <- exact_posterior(X, y, beta = 1 / log(length(y)))
  r  <- y - X %*% tp$mean
  length(y) / 2 * log(2 * pi * phi) +
    (sum(r^2) + sum(diag(X %*% tp$V %*% t(X)))) / (2 * phi)
}
w3 <- c(smc_wbic   = wbic(fit_xz)$wbic,
        exact_wbic = exact_wbic(X_xz, d$y),
        neg_log_ev = neg_log_evidence(X_xz, d$y))
w3
```

The SMC estimate is `r round(abs(w3[[1]] - w3[[2]]), 2)`
`r if (w3[[1]] < w3[[2]]) "below" else "above"` the exact WBIC. The exact WBIC
in turn sits `r round(w3[[3]] - w3[[2]], 2)` below the exact negative log
evidence, a difference that belongs to WBIC itself: it shares the asymptotic
expansion of $-\log p(y)$ up to terms that stay bounded as $n$ grows
(`?wbic`). Refitting at four sample sizes shows the gap staying bounded while
the evidence itself grows with $n$:

```{r wbic-n, fit = c("gap")}
gap <- sapply(c(30, 100, 300, 1000), function(m) {
  set.seed(2)
  dm <- data.frame(x = rnorm(m))
  dm$y <- 0.5 + dm$x + rnorm(m, sd = 0.8)
  f <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = dm, mode = "smc", phi = phi,
             beta_prior = list(mean = 0, sd = s),
             control = list(wbic = TRUE, seed = 1L))
  c(n = m, wbic = wbic(f)$wbic,
    neg_log_ev = neg_log_evidence(model.matrix(~ x, dm), dm$y))
})
round(t(gap), 2)
```

From 30 to 1,000 observations the negative log evidence rises from
`r round(gap["neg_log_ev", 1], 2)` to `r round(gap["neg_log_ev", 4], 2)`, and
WBIC stays between
`r formatC(min(gap["neg_log_ev", ] - gap["wbic", ]), format = "f", digits = 1)`
and
`r formatC(max(gap["neg_log_ev", ] - gap["wbic", ]), format = "f", digits = 1)`
below it.

## Ranking nested models

A gap of this kind cancels when two models of the same data are compared, as
long as it is similar for both. `compare_models(criterion = "wbic")` ranks fits
by WBIC; `delta` is the gap to the best model and `weight` the model weight
read off each WBIC as a log evidence. Fit the model without `z`, which is
missing a real effect, and the model with `w` in place of `z`, which adds a
covariate with no effect:

```{r fit-nested, fit = c("fit_x", "fit_xw")}
smc_fit <- function(f) {
  tulpa(f, data = d, mode = "smc", phi = phi,
        beta_prior = list(mean = 0, sd = s),
        control = list(wbic = TRUE, seed = 1L))
}
fit_x  <- smc_fit(y ~ x)
fit_xw <- smc_fit(y ~ x + w)
compare_models(x = fit_x, xz = fit_xz, criterion = "wbic")
compare_models(x = fit_x, xw = fit_xw, criterion = "wbic")
```

`criterion = "loglik"` ranks the same fits by the log evidence each SMC run
estimated:

```{r rank-evidence}
compare_models(x = fit_x, xz = fit_xz, xw = fit_xw, criterion = "loglik")
```

The exact negative log evidences give the size of the two steps: what adding
`z` gains, and what adding `w` costs.

```{r exact-rank}
nle <- c(x  = neg_log_evidence(model.matrix(~ x, d), d$y),
         xz = neg_log_evidence(X_xz, d$y),
         xw = neg_log_evidence(model.matrix(~ x + w, d), d$y))
fits <- list(x = fit_x, xz = fit_xz, xw = fit_xw)
ev <- sapply(fits, function(f) as.numeric(logLik(f)))
wb <- sapply(fits, function(f) wbic(f)$wbic)
steps <- rbind(exact    = c(nle[["x"]] - nle[["xz"]], nle[["xw"]] - nle[["x"]]),
               evidence = c(ev[["xz"]] - ev[["x"]], ev[["x"]] - ev[["xw"]]),
               wbic     = c(wb[["x"]] - wb[["xz"]], wb[["xw"]] - wb[["x"]]))
colnames(steps) <- c("xz_gain", "w_cost")
round(steps, 2)
```

```{r seeds, fit = c("wbic_seeds"), include = FALSE}
wbic_seeds <- sapply(2:4, function(k) {
  f <- tulpa(y ~ x + w, data = d, mode = "smc", phi = phi,
             beta_prior = list(mean = 0, sd = s),
             control = list(wbic = TRUE, seed = k))
  wbic(f)$wbic
})
```

Both estimates order the three models as the exact evidence does. The SMC
log evidence is within
`r round(max(abs(steps["evidence", ] - steps["exact", ])), 2)` of the exact
steps, and WBIC within
`r round(max(abs(steps["wbic", ] - steps["exact", ])), 2)`. Refitting the
`x + w` model under three more seeds moves its WBIC by at most
`r round(max(abs(wbic_seeds - wb[["xw"]])), 2)`.

## Where each estimate is available

A Laplace fit of the same model also reports a log evidence, which is exact
for a Gaussian likelihood with fixed `phi`:

```{r laplace, fit = TRUE}
fit_lap <- tulpa(y ~ x + z, data = d, mode = "laplace", phi = phi,
                 beta_prior = list(mean = 0, sd = s))
c(laplace = as.numeric(logLik(fit_lap)),
  exact   = -neg_log_evidence(X_xz, d$y))
```

An SMC fit reports no evidence when a prior has no normalizing constant, as
for an intrinsic second-order random walk. `logLik()` then returns the mean
log posterior density over the draws, with `quantity = "log_posterior_mean"`
(`?logLik.tulpa_fit`).

Only the SMC path visits the tempered posterior, so `wbic()` refuses a fit from
any other mode, and `control$wbic` is refused outside `mode = "smc"`:

```{r wbic-error, error = TRUE}
wbic(fit_nuts)
```

## Settings

Three `control` entries steer the sampler:

- `n_particles` (default 1000) is the population size. The Monte Carlo error
  of every mean and of WBIC shrinks with it, and the run time grows with it.
- `smc_min_moves` (default 1) and `smc_max_moves` (default 50) bound the
  number of moves after each step. The sampler chooses the count between
  them, and equal values fix it.
- `ess_threshold` (default 0.5) is the effective sample size the next
  temperature is chosen to keep, as a fraction of `n_particles`. A higher
  value takes more, smaller steps.

`seed` fixes the sampler's random stream, so a fit with the same data,
settings and seed returns the same draws. `n_chains`, `n_iter` and `warmup`
belong to the chain-based samplers: `n_chains` is refused on this path, and
the other two are not read.
